summary: Defines a framework and requirements for a mechanism by which a network access server controls an access node, such as a DSLAM, in broadband multi-service networks. It allows direct device-to-device communication for service, quality of service and subscriber operations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The big office talks directly to the little street-corner box that connects homes, without going through a middleman.

questions: what is an access node control mechanism
what are multicast white and grey lists
subtitle: Why DSL access nodes need to talk directly to the network access server, and what that control protocol must be able to do.

tldr.problem: In DSL broadband networks, quality of service and service control need tight coordination between the Access Node (such as a DSLAM) and the Network Access Server (NAS), but going through element managers and operations systems is impractical.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines an Access Node Control Mechanism, a direct device-to-device channel between NAS and Access Node. It describes the architecture and use cases, and then lists numbered requirements (R-1 to R-124) for the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP) and the network elements.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework and requirements document, not the protocol itself. The actual protocol specification is out of scope.

facts.label: Scale target
facts.value: A NAS controls at least 5000 Access Nodes

today: RFC 5851 is an Informational RFC (May 2010) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states the framework and requirements, while the protocol itself is specified elsewhere.

sections.title: Why an Access Node Control Mechanism
sections.content:
DSL is widely deployed for broadband access, and Broadband Forum documents (TR-058, TR-059, TR-101) describe the architectures. Traditional designs use a Permanent Virtual Circuit per subscriber, and management is split across departments that run the local loop, the ATM network and the IP network. Management networks are usually not designed to move management data between these entities in real time.

Value-added services need special attention to quality of service and service control. That calls for tighter coordination between the Access Node (AN, for example a DSLAM) and the Network Access Server (NAS, often called a BNG or BRAS), without loading the Operational Support System (OSS) with impractical expectations.

The Access Node Control Mechanism is therefore a direct device-to-device communication that does not pass through distinct element managers. This document gives a framework, identifies use cases that justify it, and lists requirements for the Access Node Control Protocol (ANCP). The requirements are based on Broadband Forum work in TR-147. The framework targets DSL access, over ATM or Ethernet, and is meant to stay open to other access technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the street box and the central office talk through lots of office departments that do not hear each other quickly. This plan lets the two boxes talk straight to each other.

sections.title: Reference Architecture
sections.content:
Subscribers' Customer Premises Equipment connects through a Home Gateway over an access loop to the Access Node, then through an aggregation network to the NAS and on to a regional network. The architecture builds on TR-059 for ATM aggregation and TR-101 for Ethernet aggregation, with the main focus on TR-101.

Three functions are defined. A controller function, typically in the NAS, requests information or triggers behavior. A reporting function conveys status, such as the access-loop data rate sent from the AN so the NAS can shape traffic to that rate. An enforcement function carries out remote actions on the AN, such as starting a port test or honoring or denying a multicast join. Both reporting and enforcement typically live in the AN.

The Control Channel is a bidirectional IP interface between the controller and the reporting/enforcement function, configured rather than discovered. The messages must not get lost, so they are typically sent over a dedicated ATM PVC or a dedicated VLAN with high priority, and the channel can share the subscriber traffic's physical network. Interactions must be reliable and, for some use cases, transactional (request and response), so that elements stay in a known state. Existing management must keep working, and conflicts between an Element Manager and ANCP must be avoided.

To tie parameters to an Access Port, the NAS needs a circuit addressing scheme. This document reuses the TR-101 scheme: a one-to-one VLAN assignment model, or a many-to-one model that encodes port and circuit in the Agent Circuit ID sub-option of DHCP or PPPoE messages.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a boss at the central office and a helper in the street box. The boss asks questions, the helper reports news and does what the boss says, and their messages get a fast lane so they are not lost.

sections.title: Non-Multicast Use Cases
sections.content:
Access topology discovery lets the NAS learn the access network's links and rates so it can do hierarchical scheduling and shaping without relying on an OSS. DSL line rates change, for instance after the line resynchronizes, so the AN sends an Information Report message to the NAS when that happens and each time attributes change above a threshold. Reported characteristics include DSL type, framing mode, port state, and actual and configured net data rates. The NAS MUST be able to receive them and share them with AAA or policy servers.

Access-loop configuration lets the NAS change a subscriber's loop parameters, such as rate or interleaving delay, without a costly business-to-business transaction between an ISP and an Access Provider. The best method is profiles pre-configured by the Element Manager, which the NAS selects with a Configure Request message. If the adjacency is down, the NAS should report the failure to the external management system.

Remote connectivity test lets the NAS trigger an access-loop test on the AN, for example generating ATM F4/F5 loopback cells, or a port synchronization and administrative test on Ethernet. The AN returns the result in a Control Response message. This keeps ATM-style troubleshooting available until end-to-end Ethernet OAM is more widely supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The street box tells the boss how fast each home's line is running right now. The boss can ask it to change a home's speed setting, or to test whether a line is working.

sections.title: Multicast Use Cases
sections.content:
For IPTV, multicast is more efficient if the Access Node and aggregation nodes take part in replication (for example with IGMP snooping or proxy), and the NAS, aggregation node and AN then have to behave as a single logical device. ANCP carries the information needed for that.

Conditional access. The NAS can provision each Access Port on the AN with a white list (flows allowed), a black list (flows not allowed) and a grey list (flows for which the AN asks the NAS before replicating). On a join, the most specific match wins, and on a tie the black list beats the grey list, which beats the white list. A join matching no list should be discarded, and a catch-all entry such as <S=*,G=*> changes that default.

Admission control. The access line must not be oversubscribed, so bandwidth checks are needed. The AN can query the NAS, or the NAS or a policy server can delegate a share of bandwidth to the AN for multicast admission control. The AN can ask for more (stating a minimum and a preferred amount) and can release unused bandwidth, and the NAS can reduce the delegation but must not go below what is in use. Unknown streams can be accepted without admission control if they are marked best effort.

Accounting and reporting. The AN can tell the NAS when replication starts and ends (basic) and add a byte count when it ends (detailed). The NAS can query which flows go to which ports.

Spontaneous admission response. The NAS can send an Admission Response without a prior request, for example to stop a flow when prepaid credit runs out or after a content preview.
sections.plainLanguage: For TV channels, the street box keeps lists: channels a home may watch, may not watch, and ones it must ask the boss about. It also keeps track of how much line room is left so too many shows do not squeeze in.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements are numbered R-1 to R-124. The general ANCP ones say it MUST be extensible through new message types or TLVs (R-1), flexible across ATM and Ethernet (R-2), reliable (R-3), and support request/response transactions that are atomic (R-4). It MUST scale so one NAS can control at least 5000 Access Nodes (R-5), and be manageable, for example via SNMP (R-6). R-7 to R-23 cover the multicast capabilities. Capability negotiation of supported use cases is required (R-27), as is an adjacency protocol with automatic loss detection (R-28, R-29). A loss of adjacency MUST NOT affect subscriber connectivity (R-30). ANCP MUST use the IP protocol stack (R-34), with IPoA encapsulation over ATM and IPoE over Ethernet (R-35, R-36).

Separate sections list what an AN and a NAS should do. For these the RFC says it does not intend to impose absolute requirements, so the words must and should are not capitalized. Examples: an AN must support at least 2 partitions and should support 8 (R-37); ANCP operations should complete in the order of tens of milliseconds (R-73, R-111); the NAS must shape traffic to an access loop to the net data rate learned from the AN (R-81); and the NAS must not drop PPP or DHCP sessions just because the adjacency goes down (R-87). Parameters such as DSL noise margin and PSD can be changed only through the Element Manager, and the EMS decides which parameters ANCP may change (R-75, R-76). Wholesale requirements cover reporting to a retail provider and L2TP (R-113 to R-116), and management requirements cover configuration and traps (R-117 to R-122).
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say the boss and the street box must say hello, notice if the other one disappears, keep the homes online anyway, and never let one side change settings it is not allowed to touch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 5713 lists the ANCP security threats and requirements, and ANCP MUST comply with them (R-123). Because multicast join and leave requests from end users trigger ANCP activity, they could be used for denial-of-service attacks on the AN or NAS. The RFC says this is not a new class of risk compared with IGMP messages sent to the NAS when the AN does no snooping.

To mitigate, the AN MAY limit how many multicast flows a user can join at once or the rate of joins and leaves. Mask-based black list entries can also deny joins for invalid flows at the AN without any ANCP exchange. The Access Node MUST NOT allow Access Node Control messages to be sent toward the customer premises (R-124).
sections.plainLanguage: Someone might keep pressing the channel button very fast to overload the boxes. The street box can limit how fast and how often, and it never sends its private messages into people's homes.
